code.pivot_mechanism:
PLAIN PIN-IN-OPEN-U, DROPPED STRAIGHT DOWN FROM ABOVE. No snap, no notch, no cradle, no closed hole.

STAND SIDE (loading_fixture.rs:84-100): two forked towers at y=-7.0 and y=+7.0. Each tower top is a U formed by two prongs, x -4..-2 and x +2..+4, z 24..30. Slot = 4.000 mm wide in X, 6.000 mm deep, floor z=24.000, mouth z=30.000, opening upward only. Each slot is only 4.0 mm long in Y (the prong thickness); the two slots are 10.000 mm apart inner-face-to-inner-face (y=-5 to y=+5) and 18.000 mm outer-to-outer (y=-9 to y=+9).

LEVER SIDE (loading_fixture.rs:140-146): "lever-axle", a cylinder from [0.0,18.5,1.5] to [0.0,32.5,1.5], radius 1.5, CYLINDER_SIDES=16 (L12). geometry.rs:1106-1158 shows cylinder == 16-gon prism with vertices AT the radius: for a Y-axis pin u=(1,0,0), v=(0,0,-1), so vertices land exactly on x=+/-1.5 and z=0.0/3.0. So the pin is 3.000 mm across corners in X (and in Z), 2.9424 mm across flats, and 14.000 mm long in Y.

FIT NUMBERS: 4.000 slot - 3.000 pin = 1.000 mm diametral clearance, 0.500 mm per side (X). Seated pin axis sits at z = 24.0 + 1.5 = 25.500 (corner-down; 25.471 if it rocks onto a facet). The pin is 14.0 mm long against an 18.0 mm outer tower span, so it does NOT bridge the towers - centred on y=0 it laps only 2.000 mm into each fork (pin ends at y=+/-7.0, exactly the tower centrelines). Axial (Y) float before one end drops out: +/-2.000 mm. Beam (3.0 mm wide in Y) sits in the 10.000 mm gap between towers with ~3.5 mm slop per side.

ENTRY ORIENTATION: the lever seats in EXACTLY its printed orientation - no rotation of any kind. Beam horizontal, long axis along X, mass peg pointing UP (+Z), paddle end pointing +X toward the receivers, both pins horizontal along Y. Align the x=0 pin over the two fork mouths (needs +/-0.5 mm X accuracy, +/-2 mm Y) and lower it straight down 6 mm into the slots. Nothing interferes on the way in: the towers occupy |y| = 5..9 while the beam occupies only y ~ -2..+1, so the beam passes cleanly between them.

Y CENTRING (this is what looks wrong by eye): the pin is NOT centred on the beam. Beam y 23.5..26.5, pin y 18.5..32.5 -> the pin protrudes 5.000 mm on the -Y side of the beam and 6.000 mm on the +Y side (the +Y side is the tab side). To get equal 2 mm engagement in both forks the pin must be centred at y=0, which puts the beam at y -2.0..+1.0, i.e. 0.5 mm off the tower centreline. Either Y facing works; the beam just sits 1 mm off-centre if flipped.

RETENTION: gravity plus load direction only. There is no clip, collar, shoulder, chamfer, lead-in, detent, or keying anywhere. The design intent is that the load path presses the pin DOWN into the open U (see lever_feature_map), which is why an open U was acceptable for a support-free grounded print. The manifest treats unseating as an expected failure mode: handling outcome "fixture_unseated" (plate.rs:918) and stop rule "...lever unseating..." (plate.rs:894).
code.lever_feature_map:
All X measured in the code's fixture frame; the pivot is x=0. (loading_fixture.rs:131-163)

x = -12.0   beam tail end (beam cuboid starts here)
x = -11.75..-8.25  MASS PEG footprint (16-gon, r=1.75, so 3.500 mm across corners), centre x = -10.000, y=25.0, z=0..12.0. Rooted 3 mm inside the beam, 9 mm proud above the beam top. Peg is 0.25 mm proud of each beam side face (beam is 3.0 wide, peg 3.5). LOAD ARM = 10.0 mm (L204, plate.rs:887).
x = -7.0..-3.0   breakaway tab A (4 mm wide, z 0..1.5, on the +Y face y 26.5..33.0)
x = 0.0     PIVOT PIN "lever-axle", 16-gon r=1.5 (3.000 across corners), y 18.5..32.5 (14.0 long), axis z=1.5
x = +28.0..+32.0  breakaway tab B (4 mm wide, z 0..1.5, +Y face)
x = +40.0   CONTACT PADDLE "lever-specimen-paddle", geometrically IDENTICAL to the pivot pin (same r=1.5, same 14.0 mm y-span 18.5..32.5, same axis z=1.5). SPECIMEN ARM = 40.0 mm (L205, plate.rs:888).
x = +42.0   beam tip (only 0.5 mm past the paddle's own corner at 41.5)

Ratio: mechanical_ratio = 0.25 = 10/40 (plate.rs:889); F_specimen_N = mass_g/1000 * 9.80665 * (10/40) (plate.rs:892). Target masses 20/40/80/160/320 g -> effective 5/10/20/40/80 g (plate.rs:890-891).

MATCHING STAND X POSITIONS: cross rails under x=0 (the pivot), x=58 and x=64 (the receivers) - loading_fixture.rs:74-80. Receiver "18" at x=58 (label at x 54.0..57.75), receiver "24" at x=64 (label at x 62.0..65.75). Both receivers place the coupon terminal at x~40.5, i.e. under/at the paddle (comment L102-103, manifest.rs:249-250).

CLASS-1 LEVER SIGN: mass hangs at x=-10 (one side), specimen contact at x=+40 (other side). A downward pull at -10 drives the paddle UP. Equilibrium therefore requires the specimen to push DOWN on the paddle (paddle bears UP on the underside of the coupon terminal), which is what presses the pin into the open U with 1.25x the applied weight. The opposite arrangement (paddle bearing down on the terminal from above) has no equilibrium at all - both moments act the same way.

The lever carries NO marking distinguishing the pivot pin from the paddle pin. digit() only knows the glyphs 1,2,4,8 (L252-260) and is used only for the stand labels.
code.carrier_cuts:
TOTAL CUTS IN THE WHOLE FIXTURE: TWO. Both are on the lever.

1. "lever-breakaway-tab-0" centred x=-5.0: cuboid [-7.0, 26.5, 0.0] -> [-3.0, 33.0, 1.5] (loading_fixture.rs:133-139)
2. "lever-breakaway-tab-1" centred x=+30.0: cuboid [28.0, 26.5, 0.0] -> [32.0, 33.0, 1.5]

Each tab is 4.0 mm wide (X) x 6.5 mm long (Y) x 1.5 mm thick (Z), lying in the bottom half of the beam (z 0..1.5), bridging the beam's +Y side face (y=26.5) to the lever carrier (y=33.0). Cut at the beam end and dress flush to y=26.5. The tabs are at x=-5 and x=+30 - i.e. NOT adjacent to either pin - so leftover tab stubs cannot physically block the pivot slot; they would only foul something at x=-5/x=+30, where the stand has nothing.

DO NOT CUT: the comb. Despite the protocol calling it "carrier-retained" (manifest.rs:243-244), the comb's 55x12x1.5 slab IS the comb body: all three tooth pairs and the four 4:1 marker bars are rooted on top of it at z=1.5 (loading_fixture.rs:167-188). There are no breakaway tabs anywhere on the comb. Cutting it destroys the gauge.

HIDDEN NEAR-BRIDGES TO INSPECT AND DRESS: both pins end at y=32.500 while the carrier starts at y=33.000 - a 0.500 mm air gap, over the pins' full z 0..3 (loading_fixture.rs:131 vs 140-153). Geometrically they are separate (the build asserts exactly 3 closed components, FIXTURE_COMPONENTS=3 at L14 / test L279-284), but 0.5 mm is inside normal MSLA cure-bleed range for a 3 mm-tall feature printed flat, so the pin ends very likely cured to the carrier edge. If the carrier was snapped off rather than cut, each pin end can carry a flare/stub of resin. Restore both pins to a clean 14.000 mm length with square ends.

Also inspect the pin undersides: the pins' bottom 16-gon vertex lies exactly at z=0.000, i.e. on the build plate, so the first layers of each pin are an over-cured sliver 14 mm long - expect a flattened/flared bottom facet on both pins.

CARRIER SCRAP AFTER CUTTING: lever carrier 65 x 12 x 1.5 mm, discard.
assembly_steps: 1. Print the fixture project 'home-support-loading-fixture.chitubox' as emitted - grounded, no supports, no rotation and no translation (package.rs save_and_reopen_fixture_project writes Placement{x:0,y:0,z_lift:0} and rejects any z_lift != 0). Printed coordinates therefore equal the code coordinates cited here.
2. Wash, dry completely, and FULLY cure with both carriers still attached. Do not cut anything before full cure (manifest.rs:243-245).
3. Identify the three components: the 90x36x30 stand, the 65x26.5x12 lever-on-carrier, and the 55x12x4 comb. The comb is finished - it needs no cutting at all.
4. Cut the TWO lever breakaway tabs (4 x 6.5 x 1.5 mm) at x=-5 and x=+30, where the beam's side face meets the carrier. Dress the scars flush with the beam side face. Discard the 65x12x1.5 carrier.

5. Inspect and dress both cross-pin ends. Each pin must be a clean 14.000 mm long, 3.000 mm across-corners stub with square ends and no flare from the 0.5 mm carrier gap or from the first-layer contact at z=0. This is the single most likely cause of a pin that will not drop into a 4.000 mm slot.

6. Identify which pin is the pivot: it is the pin 10 mm from the MASS PEG (the 3.5 mm vertical post). The other pin is 50 mm from the peg and is the specimen paddle. The two pins are otherwise identical - there is no keying and no mark.

7. Hold the lever exactly as it printed: beam horizontal and flat (3 mm face down), mass peg pointing UP, peg end to the -X side, paddle end to the +X side (toward the two tall receivers marked 18 and 24). Do NOT turn the beam on edge and do NOT rotate it about its long axis.

8. Position the pivot pin over the two forked towers (the short 4.0 mm-wide U slots at x=0, 30 mm tall) with the beam passing down the 10 mm channel BETWEEN the towers, and lower it straight down 6 mm until the pin bottoms on the slot floors at z=24. The pin only laps 2 mm into each fork, so centre it - each end should sit roughly over its tower's centreline. Seated pin axis height = 25.5 mm; seated beam occupies z 24..27.
9. Check seating: the beam should swing freely about the pivot with about 0.5 mm of X slop and about 2 mm of Y float, and nothing should touch the towers except the pin ends.

10. Take a cured coupon whose manifest row says detachable_for_loading=true, cut it free of its plate strip, and rotate it so its shaft is horizontal (manifest.rs:247-248). Stand its 1.5 mm-thick carrier-pad chunk on edge in the receiver pocket: floor z=5, back wall at x=60 (18) or x=66 (24), 16.0 mm between side rails, 3.0 mm pocket depth. An 18 mm coupon goes in the receiver marked 18 (x=58), a 24 mm coupon in the one marked 24 (x=64); both put the terminal crossbar (3.0 mm long, 3.0 mm dia, plate.rs:20-21) at x~40.5, at the paddle.
11. Drop a closed loop over the mass peg and let it settle against the peg's rooted base on the beam (manifest.rs:260-262). Weigh the object; F_specimen_N = mass_g/1000 * 9.80665 * 0.25.

12. Load 10 s, unload 30 s, measure residual bend, then ten load/unload cycles per level, stepping 20/40/80/160/320 g. Use the comb's 0.5/1.0/2.0 mm gaps as visual gates only. Stop on crack, whitening, brace separation, lever unseating, or >1.0 mm permanent set (plate.rs:894, manifest.rs:268-272).
fit_failure_hypotheses: THE TWO PINS ARE INDISTINGUISHABLE (most likely cause of the confusion). 'lever-axle' (x=0) and 'lever-specimen-paddle' (x=40) are byte-for-byte the same primitive: r=1.5, 16 sides, y 18.5..32.5, axis z=1.5 (loading_fixture.rs:140-153). Nothing marks which one is the pivot, and BOTH drop into the towers happily. Seating the paddle in the towers gives a nonsense lever (peg 50 mm out, beam overhanging 52 mm) which reads as 'this doesn't fit in a way I understand'. Only the pin 10 mm from the mass peg is the pivot.

THE PIN IS INVISIBLE IN SIDE VIEW. The pins' 3.000 mm across-corners height exactly equals the 3.0 mm beam thickness and their axes sit at the beam mid-plane (z=1.5), so in profile the lever is a featureless 3 mm bar. The pivot only shows as two small side-nubs. Easy to conclude the lever has no axle at all.

TRYING TO INSERT THE BEAM EDGE-ON INTO THE FORK. The fork slot is 4.000 mm wide and the beam is 3.000 mm thick, so the BEAM ITSELF slides into the slot if you turn the lever 90 degrees about its long axis. It fits mechanically and is completely wrong. Correct entry is beam horizontal, pins into the slots, straight down.

PIN LOOKS TOO SHORT FOR THE TOWERS. The pin is 14.000 mm long; the towers are 18.000 mm apart outside-to-outside (10.000 mm inside-to-inside), with only 2.000 mm of lap into each 4 mm-thick fork when centred (loading_fixture.rs:84-100 vs 140-146). Held up against the stand the pin visibly fails to span the towers, so it reads as the wrong feature for those slots. It is not - it is meant to lap only 2 mm per side.

NO AXIAL RETENTION, SO IT WILL NOT STAY PUT. 0.500 mm clearance per side in X, +/-2.000 mm of Y float, 2 mm of engagement, and an open-topped slot. Any nudge unseats it. Correctly assembled it still feels like it 'doesn't fit'. The manifest itself lists fixture_unseated / 'lever unseating' as expected outcomes (plate.rs:894, 918).

CARRIER STUBS ON THE PIN ENDS. Both pins end at y=32.500, only 0.500 mm from the carrier at y=33.000 (loading_fixture.rs:131 vs 140-153). At 3 mm feature height that gap is inside normal cure-bleed, so the pin ends very probably fused to the carrier; snapping the carrier off leaves a flare that makes the pin locally wider than 3.0 mm or non-square, and it will not drop into a 4.0 mm slot cleanly.

FIRST-LAYER FLARE ON THE PIN UNDERSIDE. Each pin's lowest 16-gon vertex is exactly at z=0.000, on the build plate, so the pins start as a 14 mm-long knife edge in the first layers - the classic elephant-foot case. The cured pin bottom is a widened flat, not a cylinder, and it will feel like it binds or like the 'axle' is really just a rib.

PINS ARE 16-GON PRISMS, NOT CYLINDERS (geometry.rs:1106-1158, CYLINDER_SIDES=16 at loading_fixture.rs:12). Vertices land exactly on x=+/-1.5 and z=0/3, so the pin sits corner-down on a flat slot floor. Rotation feels notchy/detented (facet width 0.585 mm, seat height varying 25.471..25.500) rather than like a bearing, reinforcing the impression it is not a pivot.

WRONG SLOTS ENTIRELY. The two 16 mm-wide, 15 mm-tall receiver channels at x=58 and x=64 look far more like 'slots intended to hold' something than the little 4 mm forks do. Those are coupon receivers; the lever never goes in them.

'18' LABEL IS PARTLY SWALLOWED. The right-hand pixel column of the '8' (x 57.30..57.75, rows 1-4, z 2.0..2.75) lies inside receiver #0's foot (x 57..62, y -17..3, z 2..5), so 4 of its 5 rows are absorbed into solid material (loading_fixture.rs:110-114 vs 126, 240-246). The label reads as a blob, and both labels sit on the FRONT rail (y~-17) while their receivers are at y=-7 and y=+7 - the '24' label is diagonally opposite its receiver.

GEOMETRY IS ACTUALLY NOT CLOSED: PIVOT IS ~15-17 mm TOO HIGH FOR THE RECEIVERS. Seated pin axis z=25.500, paddle underside z=24.000 with the beam level. The receiver pocket can place a coupon terminal at z=11.25 typical (5.0 floor + half of a 12.5 mm strip chunk) and at most z=20.0 (top of the rails and back wall). So the paddle can NEVER get underneath the terminal - yet the class-1 layout (mass at x=-10, contact at x=+40) requires the paddle to push UP, since a downward paddle force has no equilibrium (both moments act the same way). To even touch the terminal from above the beam must hang ~21 degrees nose-down, which also moves the contact from x=40 to x~37.4. Even a perfectly assembled fixture therefore looks impossible, which is consistent with the owner's report.

UPSIDE-DOWN IS UNDETECTABLE AT THE PIVOT. The beam and both pins are symmetric about z=1.5, so flipping the lever about its long axis seats identically - but it points the mass peg DOWN, contradicting the protocol's 'loop settles against the peg's rooted base on the beam' (manifest.rs:260-262). Peg must point up.
REVERSED IN Y. Flipping end-for-end about Z (peg toward +X) also seats fine and puts the paddle 40 mm away from the receivers.

COUPON, NOT LEVER, MAY BE THE REAL MISFIT. The receiver pocket is 16.000 mm between rails, but strips S4-BRACED and S5-TILES-CONTROLS are 18.0 mm wide (plate.rs:99-107) and their specimens are detachable_for_loading=true. Coupon chunks from those two strips are 2 mm too wide for either receiver.

NOMINAL CLEARANCE IS NOT THE PROBLEM. 4.000 slot vs 3.000 pin = 0.500 mm per side. Even at a pessimistic 0.15 mm per-surface overcure (slot shrinks to ~3.7, pin grows to ~3.3) there is still ~0.2 mm per side. If it binds, the cause is a stub, a flare, or the wrong feature - not cure swelling.
questions: Is the pivot tower height a bug? Seated pin axis is z=25.500 and the paddle underside z=24.000, while the coupon receivers cap out at z=20.0 (rails/back wall, loading_fixture.rs:105-124) and realistically present the terminal at z~11.25. For the class-1 lever to be in equilibrium the paddle must bear UPWARD on the terminal, which is geometrically impossible here. Should the towers be ~17 mm shorter (slot floor ~z=6.75 instead of 24), or should the receivers be ~15-19 mm taller? I can derive either but the code contains no statement of which is intended.

Was any axial retention intended for the pivot? The 14.0 mm pin laps only 2.0 mm into each 4.0 mm fork with +/-2.0 mm of Y float and nothing stopping it walking out. A collar/shoulder on the pin or a 18-19 mm pin would fix it; was one dropped when the 'descending hook' was replaced (comment loading_fixture.rs:154-156)?

Should the pivot pin and the specimen paddle be visually distinguishable? They are currently identical primitives with no mark, so a user cannot tell which end is the pivot. Do you want a keying feature (different diameter, a flange, or a raised 'P') added?

Is the pin-to-carrier gap of 0.500 mm (pin ends y=32.5, carrier y=33.0) deliberate, or should it be widened to ~1.5 mm? At 3 mm feature height it is very likely to cure-bridge, leaving stubs on both pin ends.

The protocol says 'Do not cut either carrier before ... cure' (manifest.rs:243-245), but the comb has no breakaway tabs at all - its carrier is its body. Is that prose wrong, or was the comb supposed to have breakaway tabs too?

Receiver pockets are 16.000 mm between rails, but the S4-BRACED and S5-TILES-CONTROLS strips are 18.0 mm wide and their specimens are marked detachable_for_loading=true (plate.rs:99-107, 1145-1160). Are those coupons supposed to fit the fixture, and if so should the pocket be widened to >=19 mm?
The right-hand pixel column of the '18' label is buried inside receiver #0's foot (overlap at x>=57, y>=-17, z 2..5). Should the label origin move to x<=53 (or the foot start at x=receiver_x+0)?

Confirm the intended Y centring: the pin protrudes 5.0 mm on the -Y (non-tab) side and 6.0 mm on the +Y (tab) side of the beam. My reading is that the pin should be centred on y=0 (beam 0.5 mm off the tower centreline) for equal 2 mm engagement. Was the asymmetry intentional, e.g. to key the assembly orientation?

stl.stand_receiving_features:
PIVOT SLOTS (the lever's receiving feature) — two open-top notches, one per fork tower.
- Towers: X[-4.000,4.000] (8.000 mm), Y[-9.000,-5.000] and Y[+5.000,+9.000] (4.000 mm thick each), solid from Z=2.000 (top of base plate) to Z=24.000.
- Notch void: X from -2.000 to +2.000 => SLOT WIDTH = 4.000 mm. Floor is a flat plane at Z=24.000 (verified flat at X=-1.9,-1,0,1,1.9 for both towers; no radiused cradle). Tower tops at Z=30.000 => SLOT DEPTH = 6.000 mm.
- Height of slot floor above stand base underside (Z=0) = 24.000 mm; above base plate top surface (Z=2.000) = 22.000 mm.
- Slot spacing: centers at Y=-7.000 and Y=+7.000 => 14.000 mm center-to-center; clear gap between the two towers = 10.000 mm (Y -5.000..+5.000); outer face-to-face span = 18.000 mm.
- Slot prong wall thickness (each side of the notch) = 2.000 mm (X -4..-2 and X 2..4).

COUPON RECEIVERS (separate from the pivot; two vertical drop-in pockets, open toward -X):

POSITIVE — the lever fits. All four governing clearances are positive:
1. Pin diameter vs slot width: 4.000 (slot) - 3.000 (pin OD) = +1.000 mm total, +0.500 mm per side.
2. Beam width vs tower inner gap: 10.000 (gap, Y -5..+5) - 3.000 (beam) = +7.000 mm total, +3.500 mm per side.
3. Pin length vs tower positions: pin spans 14.000 mm (Y -7..+7 once centered); each tower occupies Y 5..9 / -9..-5, so the pin engages 2.000 mm of each tower's 4.000 mm thickness. Positive engagement on both sides; pin does NOT reach the outer tower faces (2.000 mm short each side), which is fine for capture but means only 2.000 mm of bearing length per side.
4. Seating depth: with the pin bottomed on the flat slot floor at Z=24.000, the pin/beam occupies Z 24.000..27.000; tower tops are at Z=30.000, leaving 3.000 mm of slot wall above the beam. Retained laterally, open upward (lift-out, not captured).
5. Descent corridor: ray-cast confirms the stand has no material at Y in (-1.5,+1.5) above Z=2.000 anywhere in X < 57.000, so the 54 mm beam (X -12..42 relative to the pivot) has a clear vertical path down to its seated height. Contact pin at x=40, Z 24..27, clears the receiver walls (which top out at Z=20.000 and start at X=57.000).

stl.insertion_orientation:
Straight down along -Z, in exactly the as-printed orientation. No rotation is required.

As printed, the lever already has: beam long axis along X, pivot-pin axis along Y, beam height along Z. The stand's notch void is bounded by walls perpendicular to X (void X -2..+2) and runs through both towers along Y, and it is open at the top (+Z). That is precisely the orientation the printed lever is in.

Assembly motion after cutting the two carrier bridges at X[-7,-3] and X[28,32]: pure translation of the lever by dY = -25.000 (from print Y-center 25.000 to stand Y-center 0.000) and dX = 0 (lever-local X already coincides with stand X: pivot to stand x=0, contact pin to stand x=40 where the coupon terminal sits), then lower along -Z until the pivot pin rests on the slot floor at Z=24.000. The beam passes down the 10.000 mm gap between the two towers; the pin ends drop into the 4.000 mm-wide notches; the mass peg ends up pointing straight up, its top at Z=36.000.

Insertion is NOT possible along X or Y: the 54 mm beam cannot pass through the 4.000 mm X-void, and a pin rotated to lie along X would be blocked by the tower walls at X +/-2..4. Vertical drop-in along -Z is the only orientation that works.

verdict.decisive_numbers:
VERDICT IN ONE LINE: the lever DOES drop into the stand's slots (all pivot clearances positive, verified twice), but the assembled fixture CANNOT apply the 4:1 load — the pivot is 14.500 mm too high for the coupon receivers. Fit = yes; function = no.

A. PIVOT FIT — POSITIVE, no interference (I re-verified both from Rust source and by re-parsing the STL myself).
- Fork slot: void x -2.000..+2.000 => 4.000 mm wide; prongs x[-4,-2] and x[+2,+4] (2.000 mm each); floor z=24.000 (flat plane, no cradle); mouth z=30.000 => 6.000 mm deep; open upward only. Two towers, centres y=-7.000 and y=+7.000, each 4.000 mm thick in Y; inner gap 10.000 mm; outer span 18.000 mm. (loading_fixture.rs:84-100; my own winding-number Z-probe of the STL returns solid 0.000..24.000 at (x=0,y=-7) and (x=0,y=+7), and 0.000..30.000 at (x=+/-3,y=-7).)
- Pivot pin "lever-axle": NOT a circular cylinder — a 16-gon prism (CYLINDER_SIDES=16). My STL vertex-level dump for the pin region gives distinct X levels -1.5000 -1.3858 -1.0607 -0.5740 0 0.5740 1.0607 1.3858 1.5000 and the identical set on Z (0.0000 .. 3.0000). So: 3.000 mm across corners, 2.9424 mm across flats, 14.000 mm long (y 18.500..32.500), axis at z=1.500.
- Clearances: 4.000 slot - 3.000 pin = 1.000 mm total, 0.500 mm per side in X. Beam 3.000 mm in a 10.000 mm inter-tower gap = 3.500 mm per side. Fork engagement 2.000 mm per side when the pin is centred on y=0. Axial float +/-2.000 mm before one end leaves its fork.
- Seated: pin axis z=25.500 corner-down, 25.4712 once it rocks onto a facet (1.5*cos(pi/16)=1.4712); beam occupies z 24.000..27.000; 3.000 mm of slot wall remains above the beam.
- Even at a pessimistic 0.15 mm/surface overcure (slot -> 3.70, pin -> 3.30) there is still 0.20 mm per side. Nominal clearance is NOT the problem.
- Descent corridor clear: my probe at (x=40,y=0) and (x=40,y=-7) returns EMPTY — the stand has no material anywhere the 54 mm beam passes. Towers occupy |y|=5..9; beam occupies |y|<=1.5.

B. THE DEFECT — PIVOT 14.500 mm TOO HIGH (decisive chain, all numbers verified).
- Only 20 coupons are marked detachable_for_loading=true: 12 x B* on strip S4-BRACED and 8 x C* (CS1..CS4, CM1..CM4) on S5-TILES-CONTROLS (manifest JSON query + plate.rs:1157,1215). BOTH strips are 18.000 mm wide (plate.rs CARRIERS). NO 12.5 mm strip carries a loadable coupon — this corrects the code-derived analysis, which assumed a 12.5 mm chunk and got 11.25 mm.
- Receiver pocket: void x 57.000..60.000 (3.000 mm, sized for the 1.500 mm pad on edge), 16.000 mm between end rails in Y, FLOOR z=5.000, wall tops z=20.000. (My STL probe at (58.5,-7) and (64.5,+7) returns solid 0.000..5.000; at (61,-7) solid 0.000..20.000.)
- The 18.000 mm strip width CANNOT lie in the 16.000 mm Y gap, so it is forced vertical. Specimen sits on the strip centreline => shaft root 9.000 mm above the chunk's bottom edge => COUPON TERMINAL AXIS AT z = 5.000 + 9.000 = 14.000. (Worst/best case over all 20 coupons: BY* specimens sit at y=25.5 on an 18 mm strip spanning 19..37, so 6.500 or 11.500 => terminal at z=11.500 or 16.500. Max achievable = 16.500.)
- Terminal is a frustum COAXIAL with the shaft (plate.rs:415-425: [tx,ty,tz-1.25] -> [tx,ty,tz+1.25], r 2.4->3.0 mm dia), so after the coupon is laid horizontal the terminal axis runs along X and the paddle pin (axis Y) crosses it perpendicular — a proper crossed-cylinder point contact. Required axis separation for contact = 1.500 + 1.500 = 3.000 mm.
- CLASS-1 SIGN: mass at x=-10.000 pulls down => torque +10W nose-UP. Equilibrium requires the specimen to press DOWN on the paddle => THE PADDLE MUST BE UNDERNEATH THE TERMINAL. (Pivot reaction is then 1.25W pressing the pin DOWN into the open U — which is exactly why an open U was acceptable. The load path is internally coherent; only the height is wrong.)
- REQUIRED paddle axis z = 14.000 - 3.000 = 11.000. ACTUAL paddle axis z = 25.500. ERROR = +14.500 mm. Required fork slot floor z = 9.500 (actual 24.000); required tower top z = 15.500 (actual 30.000). Towers are 14.500 mm too tall.
- With the beam level there is 8.500 mm of bare air between the paddle underside (z=24.000) and the terminal's top surface (z=15.500). The lever cannot touch the coupon at all.
- No equilibrium exists at ANY lever angle. Torque of the contact normal about the pivot, for terminal at (40.5, 14.0): tau = 460*cos(phi) - 1620*sin(phi), and geometric contact (centre distance = 3.000) only occurs at phi = 12.86 deg and phi = 18.86 deg. Coming down from level the lever first touches at 12.86 deg, where tau = +88k (nose-UP, the SAME sense as the mass) — it is pushed back off. The one nose-down branch (18.86 deg, tau = -88k) lies on the far side of a solid interpenetration and is unreachable. The lever's only stable state is mass-end hanging straight down, paddle end straight up.
- Even the most generous seating anyone could contrive (chunk lifted to the very top of the pocket, root at z=20.000, zero grip) leaves the terminal 8.500 mm below the 28.500 mm the as-built paddle needs. There is no operator technique that recovers this.

C. SECOND DEFECT — PIN 14.000 mm IS TOO SHORT TO BOTH BEAR AND CONTACT.
- The pin ends land at y = -7.000 and +7.000 — exactly the two tower centrelines AND exactly the two receiver centrelines (58.5-18=40.5, 64.5-24=40.5; both receivers put the terminal at x~40.5, y=-7 or y=+7). So the design intends the PIN END to be the contact.
- Centred (c=0): 2.000 mm engagement in each fork, but 0.000 mm of overlap with the coupon — the contact is the pin's end edge exactly on the terminal's centre plane.
- To lap the y=+7 coupon (CS1/CM1, the protocol's first validation pair) the lever must slide to c=+2.000, which gives 4.000 mm engagement in the +7 fork and 0.000 mm in the -7 fork: single-fork support, guaranteed rock/unseat.
- Minimum pin length for 2.000 mm fork bearing on both sides plus 1.5 mm past a receiver centreline = 17.000 mm; 18.000 mm (y -9..+9) gives full 4.000 mm bearing in both forks and 2.000 mm past each receiver centreline. 18.000 mm is the correct number.

D. CROSS-CHECK RESULTS (where the two analyses disagreed, and who was right).
1. Pin shape: STL analysis said "right circular cylinder, diameter 3.000". WRONG — it is a 16-gon (verified, 9 distinct X levels). Its midplane chord check happened to land on the vertex pair. Consequence it missed: the pin sits corner-down on a flat floor, rotation is faceted/notchy (facet pitch 22.5 deg, 0.585 mm), seat height varies 25.4712..25.500.
2. Pin protrusion: STL analysis said "5.000 mm beyond each beam face". WRONG — beam y 23.500..26.500, pin y 18.500..32.500 => 5.000 mm on the -Y side, 6.000 mm on the +Y (tab) side. Code analysis correct. Verified from STL Y-levels {18.5, 23.5, 26.5, 32.5}.
3. Coupon terminal height: code analysis said ~11.25 mm assuming a 12.5 mm strip. WRONG — every loadable coupon is on an 18.000 mm strip; the number is 14.000 mm. Its "17.25 mm too tall" becomes 14.500 mm.
4. Code analysis hypothesis "coupons are 2 mm too wide for the 16 mm receiver". WRONG as an interference — the 18 mm strip width is the VERTICAL dimension; what goes in the 16 mm Y gap is the operator-chosen cut length. Not a defect; it is the seating axis.
5. STL analysis's headline "POSITIVE — the lever fits" is true but scoped only to lever-vs-stand. It never checked paddle-vs-coupon and so returned a clean bill on a fixture that cannot work. Do not act on that verdict alone.
6. Everything else the two agree on, I independently confirmed: stand 90.000 x 36.000 x 30.000; beam 54.000 x 3.000 x 3.000 (x -12..42); pins at x=0.000 and x=40.000; mass peg 16-gon r=1.750 at (x=-10.000, y=25.000), z 0.000..12.000; arms 10.000/40.000 = 4.000:1; carrier 65.000 x 12.000 x 1.500 at y 33..45; exactly TWO breakaway tabs, 4.000 x 6.500 x 1.500, at x=-5.000 and x=+30.000; comb gaps exactly 0.500/1.000/2.000; 3 connected components.
7. Both missed: the coupon pad must be pushed BACK against the pocket's back wall (x=60.000 / 66.000) for the 18.000/24.000 mm free span to land the terminal at x=40.500 on the paddle. Pad centred in the 3.000 mm pocket instead puts it at 39.750.
8. Cosmetic defects I confirmed on the STL: the '18' label's right-hand pixel column (x 57.300..57.750) is buried in receiver #0's foot (x>=57.000, y>=-17.000, z 2..5) for 4 of its 5 rows — the '8' reads as a blob. The '24' label is clean (tangent at x=62.000). On the comb, 4:1 marker bar 0 (x 23.000..24.250) is entirely inside, and bar 1 (25.500..26.750) partly inside, the 2.000 mm pair's right tooth (x 23.000..26.000) — verified from the STL X-level set {21, 23, 24.25, 25.5, 26, 26.75, 28, 29.25, 30.5, 31.75}. The fixture's own "HOME-CAL-LEVER-4TO1" identification, which the protocol gate depends on, is partly illegible.
assembly_instructions: SET-UP AND ORIENTATION. Put the stand on the bench with the raised digits '18' and '24' along the front edge nearest you. The two thin forked towers (the tallest things on the stand, 30 mm) are then on your LEFT; the two chunky slotted coupon holders are on your RIGHT. Everything below assumes that view. Note for later: the '8' of '18' is partly swallowed by the holder next to it and reads as a blob — the LEFT-hand, nearer holder is '18' (18 mm coupons), the RIGHT-hand, further-back holder is '24' (24 mm coupons).

DO NOT CUT THE COMB. The 0.5/1.0/2.0 mm go/no-go comb is finished as printed. Its 55 x 12 x 1.5 mm strip is the comb's own handle and body — every blade and every 4:1 marker bar is rooted on top of it. There are no breakaway tabs on it anywhere. Cutting it destroys the gauge. The protocol prose calling it 'carrier-retained' is wrong.

CUT THE LEVER FREE — EXACTLY TWO CUTS, NOTHING ELSE. The lever is the thin bar joined along one long side to a 65 x 12 x 1.5 mm scrap strip. There are exactly two bridges, each 4 mm wide, 6.5 mm long and only 1.5 mm thick (they sit in the BOTTOM half of the 3 mm beam). One is 5 mm to the peg side of the pivot pin; the other is 30 mm the other way. Cut both at the beam end with flush cutters or a scalpel, then dress the two scars flat with the beam's side face. Discard the scrap strip.

DRESS BOTH PIN ENDS — THIS IS THE STEP MOST LIKELY TO STOP THE LEVER GOING IN. Each cross-pin ends only 0.5 mm short of the scrap strip, over the pin's full 3 mm height. At MSLA cure-bleed that gap very probably closed, so if the strip was snapped rather than cut, each pin end may carry a flare or stub. Also, the pins' lowest edge lay exactly on the build plate, so expect an elephant-foot sliver running the pin's whole 14 mm length. Pare and sand both pins back to a clean 14.0 mm length with square ends, and knock the flat off the underside. Check with calipers: each pin must measure 3.0 mm max across, 14.0 mm long. A 3.0 mm pin drops freely into a 4.0 mm slot; a flared one does not.

IDENTIFY WHICH PIN IS THE PIVOT. The lever has two identical 3 mm cross-pins and NO mark telling them apart — both will drop happily into the forks, and seating the wrong one is the classic way to conclude 'this doesn't fit'. The pivot is the pin 10 mm from the fat vertical post (the 3.5 mm mass peg). The other pin is 40 mm from the peg and is the specimen paddle. Measure it; do not eyeball it.

HOLD THE LEVER EXACTLY AS IT PRINTED. Beam lying flat (3 mm face down), mass peg pointing straight UP, peg end on your LEFT, plain long end pointing RIGHT toward the coupon holders. Do NOT roll it 90 degrees onto its edge and do NOT turn it end-for-end. Warning: the beam is 3.0 mm thick and the fork slot is 4.0 mm wide, so the BEAM ITSELF will slide into the fork if you turn the lever on edge. It fits mechanically and it is completely wrong.

DROP IT IN. Hold the lever over the two forked towers so the pivot pin lies across both slot mouths and the beam hangs down the 10 mm channel BETWEEN the towers. Lower it straight down about 6 mm until the pin bottoms out. You need about +/-0.5 mm accuracy in the left-right direction and about +/-2 mm front-to-back. Nothing can interfere on the way down — the towers sit well outside the beam's path and there is no material anywhere under the beam. There is no snap, no click, no notch: it simply rests in two open U slots and lifts straight back out.

WHAT CORRECTLY SEATED LOOKS LIKE. Pin axis 25.5 mm above the bench; beam occupying 24-27 mm; 3 mm of slot wall still visible above the beam; the pin lapping only 2 mm into each 4 mm-thick fork (it deliberately does NOT span the towers — it stops 2 mm short of each outer face); about 0.5 mm of left-right slop and about 2 mm of front-to-back float; nothing touching except the two pin ends. The lever should swing freely. Because the pin is a 16-sided prism sitting on a flat floor, rotation feels slightly notchy — that is normal, not a fault.

CHECK THE ARMS WITH CALIPERS, as the protocol requires. Pivot-to-peg must read 10.0 mm and pivot-to-paddle 40.0 mm. If they are not 10.0/40.0, use the measured ratio and never call it a verified nominal 4:1.

LOAD THE COUPON. Take a cured coupon whose manifest row says detachable_for_loading=true (these are only the B* braced coupons and the CS/CM validity controls). Cut it free with a chunk of its 1.5 mm carrier pad still attached, about 12-15 mm of pad length either side of the shaft. Stand the pad chunk ON EDGE in the holder, shaft pointing LEFT toward the lever, with the strip's 18 mm width vertical (it will stand about 3 mm proud of the holder walls — that is correct). PUSH THE PAD FLAT AGAINST THE BACK WALL of the pocket: that is what puts the terminal at 40.5 mm, on the paddle. 18 mm coupons go in the near/left holder ('18'), 24 mm coupons in the far/right holder ('24').

NOW STOP — THE FIXTURE CANNOT BE COMPLETED AS PRINTED. With the coupon seated, the top of its terminal nose is 15.5 mm above the bench and the underside of the lever's paddle is 24.0 mm above it: an 8.5 mm gap of clear air. The paddle also needs to be UNDERNEATH the terminal to have any equilibrium at all, and it is 11.5 mm above it. Nothing you do to the seating closes this. Per protocol step 5 ('if it rocks, unseats, contacts an unintended surface, or the load path is unclear, stop'), record fixture_invalid and do not load the coupon. Photograph the gap for the run record.

IF YOU WANT A WORKING FIXTURE TODAY, without reprinting: saw the stand in two across the big open window (anywhere between about x=10 and x=50, i.e. between the towers and the holders), and set the holder half on a 14.5 mm gauge block or parallel, keeping both halves square and their front edges in line. That raises the coupon terminal from 14.0 mm to 28.5 mm, which is exactly 3.0 mm above the paddle axis at 25.5 mm — the paddle then bears up on the terminal as intended. Clamp or double-side-tape both halves down, then re-measure the two arms with calipers and use the measured values. Treat this as a deviation and record it.

IF YOU CAN REPRINT (recommended): shorten both towers by 14.5 mm — stem top from z=24.0 to z=9.5, fork top from z=30.0 to z=15.5, slot still 4.0 mm wide and 6.0 mm deep. That puts the pin axis at 11.0 mm, exactly 3.0 mm under the 14.0 mm terminal. At the same time lengthen both cross-pins from 14.0 to 18.0 mm (y -9..+9) so the pin bears fully in both forks AND reaches 2 mm past each receiver centreline. While you are in there, move the '18' label to x<=53 so it stops merging with the receiver foot, and move the four 4:1 marker bars off the comb tooth (start them at x>=27 instead of x=23).

WHEN IT IS WORKING. Drop a closed loop over the mass peg and let it settle at the peg's rooted base on the beam. The mass hangs on the LEFT of the pivot and drives the paddle UP into the underside of the coupon terminal — the coupon is loaded upward, and the reaction presses the pivot pin down into the open U with 1.25x the hanging weight, which is what keeps it seated. Weigh the whole hanging assembly. F_specimen_N = mass_g/1000 * 9.80665 * (10/40). Run 20/40/80/160/320 g, 10 s dwell, 30 s unload, ten cycles per level, comb in the specimen plane for the photos. Stop at the first crack, whitening, brace separation, lever unseating, or >1.0 mm permanent set.
nonfit_explanations_ranked: 1. THE PIVOT IS INVISIBLE IN PROFILE. The pins are exactly 3.000 mm across corners — identical to the beam's 3.000 mm thickness — and their axes sit on the beam's mid-plane at z=1.500, so the pin's top and bottom are flush with the beam. Viewed from the side the lever is a featureless 3 mm bar; the axle shows only as two small nubs on the beam's flanks. The owner is almost certainly looking for a protruding shaft and there isn't one. (Verified: pin Z levels run exactly 0.0000..3.0000, same as the beam.)

2. THE TWO PINS ARE INDISTINGUISHABLE AND BOTH FIT. 'lever-axle' at x=0 and 'lever-specimen-paddle' at x=40 are byte-identical primitives — same r=1.5, same 16 sides, same y 18.500..32.500, same axis z=1.500 — with no mark, flange, colour or keying. Both drop into the forks. Seating the paddle instead of the axle gives a lever with the peg 50 mm out and 52 mm of beam overhanging the stand, which reads as 'this obviously isn't how it goes'. The pivot is the pin 10 mm from the mass peg; there is no way to tell by eye.

3. THE FIXTURE GENUINELY DOES NOT WORK, AND THAT IS VISIBLE. Even when correctly seated, the paddle hangs 8.5 mm of clear air above the coupon terminal and on the wrong side of it, and the lever just flips paddle-end-up. Anyone assembling this correctly will conclude they have assembled it wrongly, because a correct assembly does nothing. This is a real defect, not a perception problem — see the defect assessment.

4. THE PIN VISIBLY FAILS TO SPAN THE TOWERS. Pin 14.000 mm; towers 18.000 mm outside-to-outside, 10.000 mm inside-to-inside. Held up against the stand the pin plainly falls short of the outer faces by 2.000 mm a side, so it reads as the wrong feature for those slots. It is not — it is meant to lap only 2 mm into each fork. (Though 14.000 mm is genuinely too short for a different reason — see defect 2.)

5. THE COUPON RECEIVERS LOOK FAR MORE LIKE 'THE SLOTS'. The two receivers are 16.000 mm wide, 15.000 mm deep pockets with proper walls and a floor — they look exactly like something designed to receive a part. The pivot forks are two 4.000 mm nicks in a pair of thin posts. If the owner said 'the stand's slots', there is a good chance they were trying to fit the lever into the receivers. The lever never goes there.

6. CARRIER STUBS ON THE PIN ENDS. Both pins end at y=32.500 and the scrap carrier starts at y=33.000 — a 0.500 mm gap across the pins' full 3 mm height. At MSLA cure-bleed that gap very likely closed, so snapping the carrier off leaves a flare that makes the pin locally wider than 3.000 mm or non-square, and it will not drop cleanly into a 4.000 mm slot. Feels like a fit problem; is a finishing problem.

7. FIRST-LAYER FLARE UNDER THE PINS. Each pin's lowest 16-gon vertex sits exactly at z=0.000, on the build plate, so each pin begins as a 14 mm-long knife edge in the first layers — textbook elephant foot. The cured pin bottom is a widened flat, which both binds in the slot and makes the pin look like a moulded rib rather than an axle.

8. TRYING TO INSERT THE BEAM EDGE-ON. The slot is 4.000 mm wide and the beam is 3.000 mm thick, so rolling the lever 90 degrees about its long axis slides the BEAM into the fork. It fits, it feels deliberate, and it is completely wrong.

9. NO RETENTION, SO IT NEVER FEELS 'FITTED'. 0.500 mm clearance per side, +/-2.000 mm of axial float, 2.000 mm of engagement, open-topped slot, no clip, collar, shoulder, chamfer, lead-in or detent anywhere. Any nudge unseats it. Even a perfect assembly feels like a part resting on another part rather than a part that has been fitted. The manifest itself anticipates this ('fixture_unseated', 'lever unseating').

10. THE '18' LABEL READS AS A BLOB. Four of the five pixels in the right-hand column of the '8' are absorbed into receiver #0's foot, and both labels sit on the FRONT rail while the receivers they name are at y=-7 and y=+7 — the '24' label is diagonally opposite its own receiver. Adds to the general sense that the printed part does not match what was intended.
verdict.defect_assessment:
THE GEOMETRY IS DEFECTIVE. Two independent defects, both requiring a source change and a reprint. I am not softening this: the fixture as emitted cannot perform the measurement the protocol is built around, and no assembly technique recovers it.

DEFECT 1 (blocking) — PIVOT 14.500 mm TOO HIGH FOR THE COUPON RECEIVERS.
Evidence chain, every number verified against both loading_fixture.rs/plate.rs and my own re-parse of home-support-loading-fixture.stl:
- Seated paddle axis z = 25.500; paddle underside z = 24.000 (fork slot floor 24.000 + pin half-height 1.500).
- Every coupon marked detachable_for_loading=true lives on an 18.000 mm-wide carrier strip (12 x B* on S4-BRACED, 8 x CS/CM on S5-TILES-CONTROLS). No 12.5 mm strip carries a loadable coupon.
- The 18.000 mm width cannot lie in the receiver's 16.000 mm Y gap, so it is forced vertical; the shaft sits on the strip centreline, 9.000 mm above the chunk's bottom edge; the pocket floor is z = 5.000. Coupon terminal axis therefore lands at z = 14.000, terminal top surface z = 15.500.
- 8.500 mm of clear air between paddle and coupon with the beam level.
- Worse than a gap: the lever is class-1 (mass at x = -10.000, contact at x = +40.000), so the mass torque is +10W nose-up and equilibrium REQUIRES the specimen to press down on the paddle — i.e. the paddle must be UNDERNEATH the terminal. It is 11.500 mm above it.
- Required paddle axis = 14.000 - 3.000 = 11.000 mm. Actual 25.500 mm. Error +14.500 mm.
- No equilibrium exists at any lever angle. Contact between the two 3.000 mm-diameter features only occurs at phi = 12.86 deg and 18.86 deg nose-down; the contact torque is tau = (460*cos phi - 1620*sin phi)*k, which is POSITIVE (nose-up, same sense as the mass) at the only angle reachable from the free-hanging state. The lever is pushed away and settles with the mass end straight down and the paddle end straight up. The one stable branch at 18.86 deg lies behind a solid interpenetration and, if reached by force, loads the coupon mostly along its own axis at an effective arm of 37.85 mm — not a 4:1 bending test.
- Best case over all 20 loadable coupons (a BY* specimen stood with its 11.500 mm side down) puts the terminal at z = 16.500, still 12.000 mm short. Lifting a chunk to the very top of the pocket (z = 20.000, zero grip) still leaves 8.500 mm. There is no operator technique that fixes this.
FIX: change the fork slot floor from z = 24.000 to z = 9.500 and the tower top from z = 30.000 to z = 15.500 — i.e. loading_fixture.rs:84-100, tower stem [-4, y-2, 2.0] -> [4, y+2, 9.5] and both fork prisms z 9.5..15.5. That puts the pin axis at 11.000, exactly 3.000 below the 14.000 terminal axis, and the paddle bears up on the terminal underside as the load path requires. The alternative (raise the receiver pocket floor from 5.000 to 19.5 and the walls to 34.5) also works but makes tall thin unsupported walls and raises the centre of gravity; shortening the towers is the better fix. Verify after the change that the seated beam (z 9.500..12.500) still clears everything — it does: the beam runs at |y| <= 1.5 while the coupon shaft runs at y = -7 or +7, so the beam never passes under the coupon; only the pin's end does, which is the intent.

DEFECT 2 (blocking for a valid measurement) — CROSS-PINS 14.000 mm ARE TOO SHORT.
The pin ends land at y = -7.000 and +7.000, which are simultaneously the two tower centrelines and the two receiver centrelines. That is deliberate: the PIN END is the contact against the coupon terminal. But it does not work at 14.000 mm:
- Centred (pin y -7..+7): 2.000 mm bearing in each fork, but 0.000 mm of overlap with the coupon — the contact is the pin's end edge exactly on the terminal's centre plane.
- To actually lap the y = +7 coupon (CS1/CM1, the protocol's mandated first validation pair) the lever must slide +2.000 mm, giving 4.000 mm bearing in the +7 fork and 0.000 mm in the -7 fork. Single-fork support: it will rock and unseat, which is precisely the 'fixture_unseated' outcome the manifest anticipates.
- The same trap applies mirrored for the y = -7 receiver.
FIX: lengthen both cylinders in loading_fixture.rs:140-153 from y 18.500..32.500 to y 16.500..34.500 (18.000 mm, spanning y -9..+9 when seated). That gives full 4.000 mm bearing in both forks and 2.000 mm of overlap past each receiver centreline. Minimum acceptable is 17.000 mm. Note this reduces the pin-to-carrier gap from 0.500 mm to zero — so also move the lever carrier from y=33.0 to y=36.0 (keeping its 12.000 mm width, y 36..48) and lengthen the two breakaway tabs accordingly, which incidentally cures the cure-bridging problem in defect 3.

DEFECT 3 (quality, not blocking) — PIN ENDS 0.500 mm FROM THE CARRIER. Both pins stop at y=32.500 and the carrier starts at y=33.000, over the pins' full 3.000 mm height. At that feature height 0.500 mm is inside normal MSLA cure-bleed, so the build's 3-closed-components assertion passes in the mesh but the printed part very likely cures bridged, leaving stubs on both pin ends after the carrier is snapped. Widen to >= 1.500 mm (handled automatically by the defect-2 fix).

DEFECT 4 (cosmetic, but it defeats the protocol's own identification gate) — the '18' label's right pixel column (x 57.300..57.750) is buried in receiver #0's foot for 4 of its 5 rows, and comb 4:1 marker bar 0 (x 23.000..24.250) is entirely inside, bar 1 partly inside, the 2.000 mm pair's right tooth (x 23.000..26.000). The protocol's step 1 requires the fixture to be positively identified as HOME-CAL-LEVER-4TO1 from those four bars. Move the '18' origin to x <= 53.000 and start the marker bars at x >= 27.000.

NOT A DEFECT, for the record: the pivot fit itself. 0.500 mm per side of clearance survives even 0.15 mm/surface overcure. If a printed lever will not drop in, the cause is a carrier stub, an elephant-foot flare, or the wrong pin — not the design clearance.
